description: Take Angkor Wat apart piece by piece in 3D, and read the story of the largest religious monument on earth: a 12th-century temple-mountain to Vishnu, ringed by a moat, crowned by five lotus-bud towers.

hotspots.text: The central lotus-bud spire rises 65 meters (213 ft) above the ground, the highest of the quincunx of five towers. It is entered by a famously steep staircase, and a statue of Vishnu once stood at the top.
hotspots.title: The 65-meter spire

hotspots.text: Four satellite towers surround the central spire in a quincunx. Together the five symbolize the five peaks of Mount Meru, the home of the gods in Hindu cosmology.
hotspots.title: The quincunx

hotspots.part: Churning of the Ocean of Milk
hotspots.text: The most famous of the temple's bas-reliefs runs along the east gallery wall: gods and demons churning the cosmic ocean to release the elixir of immortality, one of the longest narrative reliefs in stone anywhere.
hotspots.title: The Churning of the Ocean of Milk

hotspots.text: The stone causeway crosses the moat on the west axis. Angkor Wat faces west, unlike most Khmer temples, which is why the sunrise crowds gather on this side, looking east at the towers.
hotspots.title: The west causeway

hotspots.text: The central tower is reached by an infamously steep staircase climbing the pyramid's west face. The ascent itself is part of the symbolism: climbing toward the gods.
hotspots.title: The steep stair

hotspots.text: Hundreds of devatas, celestial dancers, adorn the temple walls, each with her own elaborate headdress and pose. They are among the most photographed details at Angkor.
hotspots.title: Devatas

hotspots.text: The monumental entrance tower on the main west axis, itself crowned with a lotus-bud prasat, frames the first view of the temple across the causeway.
hotspots.title: The west gopura

hotspots.text: Two free-standing libraries stand in the courtyard between the galleries. Their exact original purpose is still debated by scholars.
hotspots.title: The libraries

intro: No religious building on earth covers more ground than Angkor Wat: 162.6 hectares of galleries, causeways and towers, built in the early 1100s as the state temple of a god-king. This is how a mountain of stone became the soul of a nation.
page_title: Angkor Wat: Exploded 3D Model and History | Architectural Atlas

sections.body:
King Suryavarman II built Angkor Wat as his state temple in the early 12th century, dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu. It fuses two Khmer architectural ideas: the temple-mountain, a stepped pyramid for the gods, and the galleried temple, concentric rectangular courtyards. The whole complex is a model of the Hindu cosmos. The five towers stand in quincunx for the five peaks of Mount Meru, home of the gods; the walls and the great moat stand for the mountain ranges and the ocean around it.

The scale is without precedent. The temple grounds cover 162.6 hectares, making it the largest religious monument in the world by land area. A moat 190 meters wide and more than 5 kilometers around rings the complex, and it does real work: it stabilizes the temple's foundations by keeping groundwater from rising too high or falling too low. Three rectangular galleries rise one above the next toward the central spire, which climbs 65 meters above the ground. Long colonnades link the towers at each level, and the gallery walls carry some of the most extensive bas-reliefs ever carved.
sections.heading: A mountain for a god-king

sections.body:
Toward the end of the 12th century Angkor Wat was converted from a Hindu temple to a Buddhist one, and Buddhism has held it ever since. That conversion is part of why it survived. When the Khmer capital fell to Ayutthaya invaders in 1431 and the city around it was abandoned to the forest, Angkor Wat remained a living shrine while its neighbors crumbled.

Unlike most Khmer temples it faces west, toward the setting sun. Scholars have argued for a century about why, with one leading theory reading it as Suryavarman II's funerary temple: the bas-reliefs run counterclockwise, the reverse of the normal order, as rituals do at Brahminic funerals. Whatever the reason, the west front gives the temple its famous face: the long causeway across the moat, the guardian lions, and the five towers reflected at sunrise.
sections.heading: The temple that never died

sections.body:
Hollywood found Angkor in November 2000, when Lara Croft: Tomb Raider filmed there with Angelina Jolie. Much of the movie was shot at Angkor, and the production put the temples on the global pop map. Here is the wrinkle worth knowing: the film's most famous images, Lara picking her way through giant tree roots strangling ancient masonry, were shot at Ta Prohm, a different temple in the Angkor complex. The main temple of Angkor Wat appears in the film, but the jungle-temple of the popular imagination is its neighbor.

A year earlier, Wong Kar-wai gave Angkor Wat one of the great endings in cinema. In the Mood for Love (2000) closes with Tony Leung's Chow Mo-wan traveling to Cambodia in 1966, finding a hollow in an ancient temple wall, and whispering his secret into it before sealing the hole with mud. The Criterion Collection notes that the final sequence switches from recreated 1960s Hong Kong to the ruins of Angkor Wat, lifting a story of restrained longing onto a universal plane.

And beyond film, the temple is the country itself: Angkor Wat appears on the national flag of Cambodia, the only national flag in the world to feature a building so prominently.

timeline.text: King Suryavarman II builds Angkor Wat as his state temple, dedicated to Vishnu.
The temple is converted from Hindu to Buddhist use.
Ayutthaya invaders sack Angkor; the city is abandoned but the temple remains a living shrine.
Angkor is inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Lara Croft: Tomb Raider films at Angkor with Angelina Jolie.
Wong Kar-wai's In the Mood for Love closes with its final scene shot at Angkor Wat.
